data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of trained non-experts using an explicit checklist will produce more reliable judgments than a single expert on average because the checklist acts as a variance-reduction mechanism that eliminates 'stupid' mistakes (low-frequency omissions) which outweigh the expert's superior 'peak' performance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task's objective verifiability depends on emergent properties not captureable by discrete rules.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist's granularity reaches a point of 'compliance fatigue' where cognitive load induces random errors (SCR_012).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The cost of a Type II error (omission) is significantly lower than the cost of a Type I error (false pattern recognition).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The causal mechanism is the trade-off between 'Pattern-Based Error' (expert premature closure) and 'Rule-Based Error' (non-expert tunnel vision). In objectively verifiable tasks, the most frequent failure mode is the omission of a critical but simple step. The checklist raises the 'reliability floor' by ensuring 100% coverage of known critical failure points, effectively filtering out the high-variance 'slips' typical of intuitive expertise, whereas the expert's intuition, while higher in peak capability, is susceptible to cognitive biases like premature closure (SCR_006, SCR_007).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
